speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EVIDENCE OF MR. WALTER M. STEWART REQUEST BY PRIME MINISTER THAT WITNESS BE RECALLED BY COMMITTEE ON PRICE SPREADS AND MASS BUYING
speechtext:
I avail myself of the very first opportunity to speak to this chamber about a matter that affects the privileges of this house.
On Saturday last I had an opportunity of reading with a little care the evidence given by one Walter M. Stewart before the special committee on price spreads and mass buying on the 10th instant, whereupon I wrote a letter to my colleague, the chairman of the committee, in the following terms:
Ottawa, May 12, 1934. Honourable H. H. Stevens, M.P.,
Chairman,
Special Committee on Price Spreads and Mass Buying,
Ottawa.
M.v Dear Colleague:
I have had an opportunity to look through the evidence given by Mr. Walter D. Stewart before the special committee on price spreads and mass buying on the 10th instant.
[Mr. MacLean.l
It appears to me that, while at the end his evidence is somewhat uncertain, nevertheless it is quite clear that he insinuated that the government, or some members thereof, have given advance information to his competitors regarding pending changes in the excise taxes on tobacco and cigarettes. May I ask you to be good enough to have him recalled for the purpose of naming the cabinet ministers whom he desired to examine and giving all information in his possession with respect to his allegations that ministers of the crown have been unfaithful to their trust.
Yours faithfully,
R. B. Bennett.
This afternoon my colleague, the chairman of the committee, who had been engaged with the committee during the morning, handed me a letter which had been received by Mr. Norman Sommerville, K.C., counsel for the committee, dated at Montreal and reading as follows:
P.O. Box 1929, Montreal, Que.,
May 11, 1934.
Norman Sommerville, Esq., K.C.,
Price Spreads and Mass Buying Committee, House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
I told you after my examination yesterday that I was sorry for some of the things I had said. I would have liked to have asked the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Excise and the Montreal minister, Mr. Cahan, if they could tell why other manufacturers had advance information of the changes in excise duty.
I should' not have said what I did about buying governments and commissions. I wish to retract it. I was exasperated by what seemed an unwarranted intrusion into my own affairs and somewhat bewildered by unusual surroundings. I ask you to convey my apologies to the committee. I do not wish to impugn the motives or the conduct of any member of the government.
You may read this letter to the committee and make it public if you choose.
The two statements which I said would be sent to the committee are being prepared; they will be finished to-morrow when I shall enclose them.
I am interested in the growers receiving as high prices as possible but the draft agreement you submitted to me is not sufficiently definite to insure fair treatment to all. I have therefore hesitated to sign.
Yours truly,
Walter M. Stewart.
This letter bears date Montreal, Quebec, May 11, 1934. I received it only during the last hour but, notwithstanding the contents of the letter, in view of the reflections upon members of this chamber my request to the chairman of the committee still stands.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Resolutions have been sent to the clerk of the house with respect to, first, the public works bill, second, the elections bill, third, the bill providing for arrangements between farmers and their creditors, fourth, the bill amending the Farm Loans Act. There are possibly three others that arise out of the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act that I cannot deal with until after they have been disposed of. There are amending sections to the criminal code which we usually bring down as late as possible because, as the right hon. gentleman knows, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) is receiving all the time letters making suggestions. My thought is to try to get on the order paper by the end of the week an intimation of the legislation that we propose during this session. But there is a long bill, as perhaps this chamber knows, that has been disposed of by the Senate but not yet sent to this chamber. They have given a tremendous amount of time to it. I should say "another place," one of my colleagues suggests. It has been considered by the other house, it will reach here I think this week, perhaps to-morrow or the next day.
Then there is a bill consolidating the Excise Act, about which I spoke some weeks ago, but which is not being submitted to the house until such time as the resolutions being adopted under the budget are passed, so that the Consolidated Excise Act will not be brought down to-day. I do not think it will be disputatious, because the changes are very few. Perhaps the right hon. gentleman knows that a great many regulations have been issued under the provisions of the Excise Act and it is desirable to adopt the suggestion made the other day-perhaps not for that reason-to embody in that legislation what were regulations, so that the public may be able as far as possible to see them. I may' say that the present views of the right hon. gentleman in that regard were not his views at the time the consolidation of the Excise Act last took place, but we all change our views as occasion necessitates, and I think in the case of the Excise Act it is desirable that there should be every intimation to the public.
Beyond that I do not think there will be any legislation, but I shall give the house the fullest information with respect to that by the end of this week.
I am obliged to the right hon. gentleman, and those on this side of the house appreciate to the full his courtesy in suggesting that if the program of legislation is made known it might expedite the business of the house, but I think he will not regard it as unfair if I say that I think some legislation at least might have been hastened a little during the last ten days.

Did I
understand the Prime Minister to say that the amendments to the Finance Act, the Dominion Notes Act and the Currency Act will not be introduced to the house until the Bank Act is disposed of?

With the consent of the house I move that the house go into committee of supply merely for the purpose of considering some interim supply of which I hope the house will approve. If this motion is carried then I shall make a short statement regarding it.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Cape Breton) in the chair.

I have a resolution here asking for interim supply. The main reasons why we have come to the house at this time are two: the House of Commons estimates, and the seasonal requirements of the various departments. Only one-sixth of the House of Commons estimates have been voted, and that money has been spent on account of the activities of the committees, and further money is required for that purpose, as hon. gentlemen will no doubt readily understand.
Then there are some items of public works which the department is anxious to get on with because this is the time of year when they are able to make the best progress. If there are any items which hon. gentlemen wish to discuss I shall try to give any explanations I can. But they are all brought up owing to the season of the year and the desirability of making as much progress as possible in the spring. Further, I may say that out of these various items there are only six which refer to estimates which have not

already been considered and passed by this house in their entirety. Of course the house will retain as usual the right to discuss these items as much as hon. gentlemen wish when they are brought before the house.
There is also schedule B to this resolution which refers to the Canadian National Steamships and the Maritime Freight Rates Act. That was not in the original estimate as printed, and no part of it has yet been voted. All I am asking for to-day is three-twelfths, the same as for the other estimates.
I have taken advantage of this opportunity to include in this resolution another one-twelfth of the main estimates. The reason for that is that the provision already made will expire at the end of this month, and so it seemed desirable to put in this bill another one-twelfth of the main estimates, which would carry us to the end of June, in the hope that before then the house will have prorogued.

The right hon. gentleman was kind enough to confer with the ex-Minister of Defence and with myself in regard to this interim supply. I think the house will find that the items are satisfactory, and it is appropriate that they should be passed at this time. There are one or two questions that we shall wish to ask in regard to some of the items, and perhaps they can be taken up as the items are called.

Can the minister tell us how many investigators are working throughout the country in connection with price spreads?

I could not answer that question offhand. Certain individuals have been retained to carry on investigations into details and report to the committee, in order to save the time of the committee and to avoid bringing more witnesses than is absolutely necessary. I may say that the amount of business and the demands made upon the committee have been so enormous that there is no possible hope of -covering all the ground. I think that is clear to everyone, whether or not they are members of the committee, but the committee is doing its best to carry out its very heavy task as expeditiously as possible.
May I ask the minister if he anticipates that the deliberations of the committee will be concluded before the end of the present session of parliament?

Certainly, and a substantial report can be made as to the ground that has been covered, but it is easily seen that many phases of mercantile activity cannot possibly be covered by this committee or by any other body except over a very lengthy period.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 64, respecting Dominion Companies.
Explain.

This bill is a revision of the acts relating to dominion companies and has been prepared with very considerable care. It is a bill which, I think, will not provoke any party or partisan discussion because it is an expression of a desire to provide such a consolidation and such amendments and modifications of the provisions of the Companies Act, now existing, as may be required to satisfy changes which inevitably take place from time to time in public opinion with regard to public companies.
I have had some forty years' experience in dealing with company legislation, and I can only assure the house that, after consideration of all the representations made to the Department of the Secretary of State during the past two years, this bill embodies what appears to me to be a just and comprehensive revision of that act.
So far as the policy and principle of the bill is concerned, that simply assumes, on voting for the second reading, that the house is in favour of a prospective consolidation and a prospective revision, and when the bill comes before the committee of the whole house, to which I shall move that it be referred, it will be open to full and detailed discussion.
My own experience is that it is very difficult indeed, in committee of the whole house, to prepare amendments during the discussion of a bill, because one has then in view a particular section or particular sections which are under discussion, without regard to the import and application of other sections of a complex measure. I remember that not long ago, in absolute good faith, I assured the 
right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), in discussion in the committee of the house, that an amendment which he suggested and which I then drew would fulfil all the requirements which he had indicated. I so stated in the utmost good faith. It has become necessary to grant a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada for a decision on that very issue, and I confess that when I was giving the right hon. gentleman that assurance there was one aspect of one section of an existing act to which my attention had not been directed and which, if my attention had been so directed, might have resulted in my making the proposed amendment more comprehensive and detailed than was the amendment which I then suggested and which carried.
If therefore I may now state my view, it is this. I should like this bill to be read the second time and the house to go into committee and perhaps pass the first and second sections-

That, I suppose, is impossible but I should like to meet the serious views of the majority of the members of the house with regard to the modifications that should be made in the Companies Act.
With that in view, and with an assurance to the house of our desire to place this bill on such a basis that party or partisan discussion will not be necessary, but rather that we may seek to elicit a coordination of the views of the whole house with regard to the complex provisions of the bill, so far as possible, I now move the second reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire before the discussion is proceeded with, to rise to a point of order concerning the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) which appears at page 2445 of Hansard and reads as follows:
This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance give no indication of the intention of the government to abandon the policies of economic nationalism which have proved so disastrous to Canada's trade.
It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote export trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of conditions in Canada, and to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment designed to effect this end.
I desire to take objection to the latter part of the amendment and to show that it is out of order inasmuch as it deals with matters which have already been dealt with by the bouse. The particular words to which I invite Your Honour's attention are these:
And to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment designed to effect this end.

The Budget-Point oj Order
The end being presumably the increasing of export trade. It is difficult to determine to what extent export trade will be affected by credit unless we discuss credit as well as export trade. The other day the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) took objection on similar grounds to a subamendment; he called attention, as I do now, to a resolution which was moved by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas), and in which the following words appear:
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to the creation of a national system of credit and finance.
And the subamendmemt was ruled out of order because in it these words appear:
And further, that this house is of the opinion that the control of national credit, which by the constitution is vested in this parliament, should be exercised immediately by the government.
The hon. member argued that on those grounds, namely, that credit was mentioned in the resolution moved by the hon. member for Camrose and that it was again mentioned in the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), the said subamendment was therefore out of order. I draw your attention, sir, to the ruling which you gave sustaining that particular contention and I quote your words in giving your ruling.
I am of the opinion that the objection to the subamendment is properly raised, as it seeks to deal with a matter already discussed at this session, and one which is at the present time referred to the select standing committee on banking and commerce. I therefore find the subamend'ment to be out of order.
If the question of credit as mentioned in our amendment was before the banking and commerce committee and therefore rendered our subamendment out of order, surely the fact that credit is also included in the main amendment moved by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth causes it to be out of order. Further I would suggest that Your Honour should consider the amendment of the hon. member to whom I have referred, in the light of paragraph 397 appearing on page 127 of Beauchesne's Rules and Forms, as follows:
An amendment must not raise any question which by the rules of the house, can only be raised by a distinct motion after notice.
In other words the question of credit mentioned in the amendment is a substantive motion and does not refer to any particular part of the matter with which the budget deals. Therefore I would suggest that on both these grounds the matter cannot be discussed

again in the amendment: first, that the question of credit is being dealt with by the banking and commerce committee under two measures, one the ordinary revision of the Bank Act and the other, dealing with the question of a central bank; secondly, that it is a substantive motion of which notice should have been given, and that it is not germane to the main matters with which we have to deal. I would also say that the whole question of unemployment, which is mentioned in the amendment I have just quoted, has been dealt with by this house on a motion of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) on February 7, 1934, namely:
That, in the opinion of this house, in view of the large number of unemployed, and with the necessity of increasing the purchasing power of the people, it is expedient that the government give immediate consideration to the inauguration of a large scale program of public works to be financed by a direct issue of non-interest bearing dominion notes.
That includes not only the question of credit but also unemployment, both of which are mentioned in the amendment. The hon. member for Macleod discussed that resolution, which is at the present time on the order paper. Therefore, sir, I submit that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) is out of order for precisely the same reasons that our subamendment was ruled out of order the other day by yourself.

On the point of order raised by the hon. member, if I understood him aright he raised three specific issues. The first was that the question of credit referred to in the amendment is before the committee on banking and commerce, and the hon. member quoted marginal notation No. 397 to standing order 48:
An amendment must not raise any question which by the rules of the house, can only be raised by a distinct motion after notice.
At once, sir, I wish to submit that the citation of marginal notation No. 397 has nothing to do with the point of order. I think the hon. member knows that there are certain resolutions that require notice, and the mere fact of an amendment suggesting any of these questions which might come up on a substantive motion has nothing to do with the point of order.
Then the hon. member suggested that the question of economic nationalism was referred to in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), and that the question was previously disposed of in the debate on the address in

The Budget-Point of Order
reply. I suggest that after careful perusal of the motioa for an address in reply and the amendment thereto moved by the official opposition you will find that there is no reference to the words "economic nationalism." We moved an amendment adding certain words-that His Excellency's present advisers have lost the confidence of the country. Therefore that point is not germane to the present issue.
Two points remain: first, that the question of credit is now before the committee on banking and commerce, and second, that the question of unemployment was disposed of in two previous debates, on the motion of Mr. Heaps, and on that of Mr. Coote, during the present session. I submit that the other day when I raised a point of order the question of national finance or national credit was concretely before this house in the form of a specific resolution moved by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas) and was disposed of on a point of order raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). The general question of credit is always before this house and the banking and commerce committee, and therefore the reference to the word " credit " makes absolutely no difference. Then in regard to the general reference to unemployment: two resolutions were mentioned, one proposed by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps), which dealt with a specific phase of the unemployment situation and offered specific remedies according to his ideas in the way of curtailing hours of labour, the redistribution of wealth, and the increase of purchasing power.

There is one distinction between the amendment that has been moved by the official opposition and the one referred to by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, which I think should be drawn to your honour's attention. The amendment of the official opposition says nothing at all with respect to the particular policies on credit or unemployment which are referred to in the amendment. The amendment is solely to the application of any policies, whether they be the policies of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) or the policies of the official opposition. The amendment distinctly reads:
It is of the opinion that the immediate substitution therefor of policies which will promote export trade throughout the world is essential to any permanent improvement of conditions in Canada, and' to the successful application of other policies respecting credit and employment designed to effect that end.
There is no controversy in the mind of any of us as to the policies recommended by hon. gentlemen in the far corner being designed, from their point of view, to effect the end of improving conditions. We are in agreement as to that; they may be different policies from these which we are proposing, but this amendment says that it would not matter whether the policies of the members of the 'C.C.F. group or those of the official opposition were to be the policies of the day, that they could not be effectively applied unless in some way the policies with respect to export trade were of such a character as to improve trade as such. I submit therefore that there is a distinction between the two amendments that is vital, and altogether apart from discussing the previous ruling of Your Honour the amendment which is now being called in question seems to be perfectly regular inasmuch as it relates to the application of policies in general, and not to the question of specific policies with respect either to credit or to employment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :

When the other day this matter was being discussed, on the point of order then raised I asked the Speaker whether or not that applied to the whole of the subamendment, because it contained certain words about which I had the gravest doubt. I still have that doubt. The question, however, is this: Can the house twice debate and arrive at a conclusion with regard to the same matter during the same session? If the amendment proposes to review the decision already arrived at, then I think the amendment is out of order. I think we have held that too frequently to have it further discussed. The amendment of the official opposition first of all alleges what are the policies of the government and then states that the opposition favours the substitution therefor of certain other policies which are named. With respect to one of these there might be a very debatable question as to whether it has been discussed this session in the sense of a conclusion having been arrived at. When the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) was making his observations I remembered that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), following the general amendment moved by hon. gentleman opposite to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, moved an amendment which I have just read, and which I hesitate to read a second time. However, his words were:
We respectfully regret that Your Excellency's present advisers have not taken such steps as are necessary to deal adequately with unemployment, to reduce the burden imposed by the public debt, and to put the agricultural industry on a basis that will insure to the farmer a decent standard of living.
Rightly or wrongly the house divided on that question and by a vote of 54 to 89 determined for this session that the government of the day had not failed to deal adequately with unemployment, to reduce the burden imposed by the public debt or to put the agricultural industry on a basis that would ensure to the farmer a decent standard of living. Whatever in the amendment to the motion to go into supply is at variance with that in my judgment should be stricken out, following the course of reasoning that always has been adopted in parliament, namely that you never would cease to debate if you continued, sitting after sitting, to discuss a matter already disposed of. It is quite clear that when this house voted upon the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and seconded by the hon. mem-

The Budget-Point of Ordei
ber for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), for this session it did dispose of those matters; I think we all agree with respect to that. Instead of limiting the amendment to a specific matter they dealt with three broad, general policies, unemployment, agriculture and the public debt, and in connection with all three they asked that the attitude of the government be challenged. That has been done; the vote has been taken, and I do submit that this phase of the matter is disposed of.
It will be recalled that it was decided by your predecessor, Mr. Speaker, that with respect to matters that were already on the order paper an amendment could not be offered to the motion later submitted to the house. That was in connection with the natural resources debate. An effort was being made by the late hon. member for Frontenac-Addington to move an amendment on going into supply, and the resolution upon the order paper precluded him from doing so because it was held that you could not anticipate, by a motion on going into supply, a matter that was to be the subject of debate. As a matter of fact the marketing bill had been submitted to this house and had received first reading before the amendment was moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). That bill does deal with the export trade; the very title states that it is desirable to encourage export trade. Whether or not you should place a more limited construction upon those words than their broad and general meaning would indicate I am not going to argue, because last session I did indicate what I should like to repeat now: When an opposition, whether it be the official or the unofficial opposition, see fit to move amendments to the address challenging the specific policies of the government, and a vote is taken which is adverse to them, they cannot again during that session move the same amendment. That is one of the risks that must be taken. Whether or not they sufficiently amplified their position when they first moved the amendment is not for me to say, but it is obvious that they cannot move the amendment a second time on going into supply.

I do not know that there has been a carefu: decision given by the chair as to how far the discussion of these matters on the address, when a vote is taken, precludes the possibility of raising them again in somewhat different words on going into supply. I have pointed out, as I do again, that when on the address in reply to the speech from the throne you see fit to challenge the policies of the government and specify the general policies to which objection is taken, you cannot again challenge them on going into supply, and that is just what this amendment does in at least three points.
The other day I raised the question, which is still uncertain in my own mind, as to whether or not the subamendment moved by the unofficial opposition, in terms negativing the motion to go into supply by substituting for that motion a portion of the amendment moved by the official opposition, to which was added the view of the unofficial opposition as to what the policy should be, was in order. The Speaker, with the approval of the house subsequently given, ruled that this was out of order. I may say that I am wholly in accord with that view except with regard to one item; it is true that it is a small item, but in my judgment the house has not yet dealt with it.
With respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, every one, but two, of the matters contained therein has already been dealt with by this house on recorded votes, or, what is more important, those questions are now upon the

The Budget-Point of Order
order paper and open for discussion. Such procedure is precluded by a rule about which, at the time it was given by your predecessor, Mr. Speaker, I had some doubt, but which upon subsequent investigations I satisfied myself was absolutely sound, namely, that if in good faith there is placed upon the order paper-and I say in good faith, because I fancy the house would be quick to deal with a question which was merely intended for purposes of embarrassment-if a resolution had been placed upon the order paper for discussion, and then it was sought, upon amendment going into supply, to deal with it, it is out of order because you anticipate a discussion which must take place. On the two grounds the amendment-not in its entirety, in my judgment-must fall, first, because it endeavours again to revive for discussion in this house questions of which this house has disposed by recorded votes and, secondly, because in its terms it anticipates matters which are already upon the order paper, and with which this house has partially dealt and is about to continue to deal.

speechtext: Before he concludes his argument may I ask the Prime Minister a question? I would submit to my right hon. friend that if he construes the expression "matter disposed of" as applying to general conditions or to matter or matters, used in a general sense, rather than to a specific matter, there would be no opportunity for debate, discussion or amendments of any kind. It surely must relate only to specific acts or policies which have been discussed and disposed of. As an instance I would mention a motion by the opposition to the effect that the government does not any longer enjoy the confidence of the house. My right hon. friend's contention is that if that motion is moved once in a session it cannot be moved a second time whereas, as my right hon. friend knows, it may as a matter of fact be moved fifty times, if we follow the rules which have heretofore been followed. The rules must be considered in a broad and liberal way so as to permit discussion, and it is important that the Prime Minister should not place upon the words the limited and restricted interpretation which he has just given. *

Then a vote may be taken accordingly. That is a motion, which, of course, having regard to the British North America Act must always be in order. I am simply answering
that the "why not" is the reason that this is out of order. That is why not, exactly. It is not intended that at the same session the same speeches should be made on the same matter. One is on the ground of economy, and the other is that a conclusion already arrived at should not be challenged.
I am not expressing any opinion about the matter other than to indicate that as I read the rules-and I made this statement last session as I had made it before-if an opposition challenges a government's policy as reflected in the speech from the throne to the extent of moving an amendment and taking a vote, it then is precluded from challenging those same policies on a motion to go into supply, and taking a vote on the same matter. The right hon. gentleman is entirely right when he states my point is that the question is whether or not the amendment now 'before the house challenges the policy of the government on the same grounds or with respect to matters dealt with previously in the amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This is a matter of considerable importance, and one which I think should be very carefully considered.

If a resolution has been moved, seconded and passed by the House of Commons that resolution cannot again become a subject matter in a session.

speechtext: There is no distinction between specific and general; otherwise the rule would have no value. Speeches on general matters are amplified and illustrated from specific instances, and it seems to me somewhat anomalous that a man can condemn a policy of government with respect to a general program it is endeavouring to carry out, and then say, "Now, I am going to move a vote of want of confidence with respect to the same matter by taking one part from it and making it the subject matter of an amendment to go into supply." It might be made the subject matter of a motion of no confidence in another way, but that is not the matter we now have under consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my hon. friend from Cariboo (Mr. Fraser) on his interesting speech, though I shall not attempt to follow him. The hon. gentleman must be in the inner councils of the government; after listening to his purely political speech one would think there must be an election just around the corner. I am not going to answer his speech but I should like to discuss the lumber situation for a few moments.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) was in Vancouver in January he attended a meeting held under the auspices of the board of trade, and made a very good speech before a very large gathering. Just here let me say that I am not going to touch on very many subjects. I have been in the lumber business all my life, however, and a good deal has been said in this house in regard to lumber both by those who do know and those who do not know about it. During the course of his remarks the Prime Minister complimented the lumber industry of British Columbia for setting up an all time record of lumber exports during 1933. I do not accuse the Prime Minister of having made a misstatement; I believe he misunderstood the statement that was handed to him by someone, but I want to give the correct
The Budget-Mr. Munn

figures. In 1929 our exports of lumber from the dominion totalled 1,696,110,000 feet, valued at $47,663,849, or about $28 per thousand. In 1933 the total exports of lumber from Canada amounted to 619,675,000 feet, valued at about $11,098,675, or roughly $18 per thousand feet. That is the picture; in 1929 we expected about three times as much as we expected in 1933. No doubt some of the Prime Minister's friends told him we had made an all time record in that year.
Here is another feature of the situation. In 1933 we exported something over 313,000,000 feet to Great Britain and 306,000,000 feet to other countries. For the 313,000,000 feet we received $5,341,000; for the smaller amount of 306,000,000 feet we received a larger return, $5,757,000. Those are the actual figures; there is nothing political about that.
My hon. friend from Cariboo has left the chamber; I am sorry, because I am just coming to something that might be of interest to him. The hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) gave this house some interesting figures on April 23, appearing at page 2437 of Hansard, which proved beyond a doubt that while our lumber exports to Great Britain have increased we have lost a great deal of business in the way of exports to the United States. Let me give the house the lumber shipments from British Columbia to the United States for the yeajrs 1929 to 1933 inclusive:

You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that it is quite true that our exports to Great Britain have increased, but in proportion our exports to the United States have decreased very much more. To-day we are still over 300,000,000 feet short of taking up the slack of the loss of the United States market alone, to say nothing of the terrific shrinkage in the Canadian market. During 1933 our total
IMr. Munn.]
production was fifty-two per cent of the production of 1929. They tell us that in British Columbia the lumber business is booming, but that was how the production of 1933 compared with 1929, and the average sale price in 1929 was $21.50 per thousand feet, while in 1933 it was $13.50. I do>
not know why, but they say that in British Columbia the lumber business is prospering. No one in Canada would be better pleased than I if that were the case, because I am financially interested, but since I have come to Ottawa in 1930 we have done very little business in lumber. An analysis shows that the Canadian market absorbed 690,831,000 less feet of our lumber in 1933 than in 1929, and that the United States took 551,500,000 less feet in 1933 than in 1929. I notice that the hon. member for Cariboo has left the chamber; he might be interested.
Speaking in this chamber on October 26, 1932, I made the statement that in my opinion the lumber business in Canada would not get back to anything like normal conditions until we got back into the United States market. For years the Pacific coast states have been asking for a higher rate of duty or tax on Canadian lumber going into the United States, but until 1932 they could not get Washington to act. During 1931 and 1932 a very strong lobby movement was engineered by the Pacific coast states to raise the tariff or put a tax on Canadian lumber imports into that country, and finally the argument was advanced that through her imperial conference treaties Canada was raising her tariffs against the United States, through preferences granted to other countries. Let me quote some of the statements which were made in Washington in support of the proposed increase in the tariff or tax on Canadian lumber. The Pacific coast lobbyists made a very strong move for the imposition of extra tax, or duty, whichever you choose tor call it. As evidence of the points I have made I shall read from the proceedings before the Senate finance committee on the Revenue Act of 1932. I quote from the evidence of Mr. W. B. Greeley, Secretary and Manager of the West Coast Lumber Association. At page 636 of the evidence I find the following:
Mr. Greeley: What has happened, Senator Couzens, is that with the tariff and shrinkage in our home consumption, as I mentioned, with a corresponding shrinkage in our export business because of depreciated currency difficulties, and the preferential tariffs that have to-day

The Budget-Mr. Munn
practically shut us out of the British empire and all its dominions, and because of the foreign regulations and quotas that have shut us completely out of France, our industry is prostrated.
Senator Couzens:	So those are the real
reasons that you are asking this to-day?
Mr. Greeley: Those are reasons, Senator, and the real primary reason is that seventy-five per cent of our men are unemployed. Now, when you consider the communities in which these men lived, it is a very critical situation.
Senator Gore: You have no way of telling why these preferential rates were granted and the quotas cut to keep out our stuff?
In other words, lumber.
Mr. Greeley: Oh, I know the common reason that is given, or the reason that _ is commonly cited is that it was in retaliation against us in this country. I am no expert on those subjects, but I do know, so far as our tariff is concerned, there are no tariffs that keep a single pound of foreign wood pulp production out of the United States.
On the other hand, we are in a position where their preferential tariffs benefit them and they shut us out. And while our friends in British Columbia are steadily increasing their exporting business, and are running their mills at capacity, we -are shut _ off from the export business and have a shrinkage in our home market which has just reached a point where the industry is going to pieces.
Senator Thomas (Idaho): Mr. Greeley, is Russia a competitor here?
Mr. Greeley: In a mild way, Senator. They range from a maximum of 70,000,000 feet to about 14,000,000 feet in 1931, which is not, of course, an important quantity. The Russian imports of pulpwood, however, have been a very substantial factor at one time or another, and a very serious threat to our pulpwood industry.
Senator Gore: Does Canada get preferential rates in England under this new tariff?
Mr. Greeley: Yes, ten per cent.
Senator Gore: When did that go into effect?
Mr. Greeley: It went into effect on the 1st of March. The trade agreement between Canada and Australia levied a preferential tariff against America of twenty shillings per thousand feet. This is on rough lumber. That has been operating almost a year, and has kept the American lumber out of the Australian market. And the same thing is happening in Great Britain and in Africa. In other words, we have had this double burden: This shrinkage in our home market, and this competition in our home market from British Columbia. We have had a very rapid loss in our domestic market.
Then, at page 642 of the proceedings under the Revenue Act of 1932 Senator Greeley made this statement:
The preferential tariffs within the British empire, are rapidly closing many important former markets to American lumber. The trade agreement between Australia and Canada made effective nearly a year ago, gives the Canadian lumber exporter a preference of twenty shillings per thousand board feet on the usual Douglas fir items, and has largely shut out American lumber from this market.
South Africa gives Canadian lumber a preferential tariff of three per cent; Great Britain a preferential tariff of ten per cent, with every indication that it will be materially increased in pursuance of the British empire trade policy. American lumber exports to Great Britain have already shrunk materially; and that market will hereafter be practically closed to our saw mills.
At page 665 of the same proceedings, Mr. R. M. Ingram, secretary and sales manager of the E. C. Miller Cedar Lumber Company, of Aberdeen, Washington, state!:
On Grays harbour we market exports, intercoastal and rail. Our export markets are practically gone because of British empire preferential in Australia, New Zealand, England and import tariffs into Canada. Japan has been lost because of the difference in exchange, France because of quotas and embargos. Our intercoastal business is fast being superceded, what little there is left, by Canadian lumber and shingles.
The fallowing statement made by Mr. C. C. Sheppard, of the Southern Pine Association, is taken from page 11202 of the Congressional Record:
Whereas the lumber industry of the United States is now operating at approximately 20 per cent of capacity, and with the many communities in the south dependent entirely upon the saw mills, thousands of families are undergoing extreme hardship and privation because of the forced curtailment of lumber production; and
Whereas Canadian trade agreements with Australia, South Africa, England, Ireland and Scotland, preferential duties of other countries and the general depreciation of foreign currency have practically eliminated the exportation of lumber by the United States to countries which heretofore have consumed tremendous quantities; and
Whereas, with only the domestic markets remaining, and these being on an extremely subnormal basis of consumption, the lumber manufacturers are forced with the dumpage of surplusage by Canadian producers, who are protected by higher prices in British-controlled territories, and with the importations of lumber produced in Russia from confiscated timber with convict or forced labour.
Page 11278 of the Congressional Record contains the following statement by Senator Jones from Washington:
The lumber industry of the United States is now operating at approximately 20 per cent of its capacity. The object of this amendment is to provide an equalization of competitive conditions for the American forest industry. It has been stated, and I assume that it is true, that Canadian trade agreements with Australia, South Africa, England, Ireland and Scotland provide for preferential duties oyer other countries, and the general depreciation of foreign currencies has practically eliminated the exportation of lumber by the United States to countries which heretofore have consumed tremendous quantities.
The Budget-Mr. Munn

At page 11287 Senator Nye said:
One of the arguments advanced as a reason for a tariff on Canadian lumber is the preferential tariff agreements between Canada and Australia and the United Kingdom, which it is alleged shut the domestic exporter out of the Australia and English markets.
Those arguments, Mr. Speaker, were used in Washington at the time of the lobbying for an additional tax on Canadian lumber, and at a time when the lobbyists knew that the conference agreements had not been finally completed. The preference on lumber had been agreed upon in March but was to be confirmed later by treaty. I made the statement in 1932, and I make it again now, that while we of course received some benefits in the British market from those agreements, in my judgment we lost very much more in other markets which we had been enjoying for practically a lifetime.
My hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), speaking in the house on May 7, attempted to justify the lumber agreement as arrived at in Ottawa at the time of the conference in 1932. My candid opinion is, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend and his associates have up to date suffered more financial loss in connection with these same treaties than any other lumber firm in Canada, through having the American market closed to their business. However, one cannot help but admire the wonderful loyalty displayed by my hon. friend to his political party in supporting these agreements, when he and others who happen to be familiar with the situation know that he is talking against his own financial interest just to keep in line with and support his own party; and when giving figures in connection with lumber shipments, he does not give the whole story. My hon. friend who is considered the expert on lumber from the government side may be a good lumberman or may not, but we all agree that he is loyal to 'his party.

speechtext:
Before the house rose at six
o'clock I had discussed the lumber situation at some length, and there are just a few more words I wish to say in connection with it.
For many years the lumber operators in Washington, Oregon and California had lobbied for a duty on lumber from Canada. That was prior to 1982, when they were finally successful in having $3 excise imposed. The farmers in the middle west objected; they

said, "No; if you put a tax on British Columbia lumber it means that we in the middle west and consumers in the east will have to pay more for it". In my arguments before six o'clock I gave conclusively the reason why the United States government finally consented to impose an excise tax of $3 per thousand on lumber from this country, and that was a blow to the Canadian lumber industry from which in my opinion we shall not recover until we get back that market.
I am one of those who take up little of the time of this house. I believe that if a man has anything to say he should say it and get through as quickly as possible. Now, I have not much more to say and I am going to say it quickly. As a business man, I say that some of the legislation that has been passed in this house by this government is half baked. Last session the sugar tax was half baked legislation. In the first place, if the government wanted to put a tax on sugar, one cent a pound would have been reasonable; that would have been common sense. Instead they put on a tax of two cents and for some reason or other-I do not blame the Minister of Finance at all-there must have been a leak somewhere and that leak cost the taxpayers of this country four or five million dollars. That did not accrue to the benefit of consumer or producer but to the benefit of the profiteer, and that is what I call half baked legislation. I am glad to see that the Minister of Finance has decided this year to reduce the duty to one cent a pound. I would urge however that instead of having that reduction come into effect on the first of July it should take effect on the first of June. Our people in British Columbia are pretty well through with the canning business before the first of July, and if the reduction were put into effect on the earlier date I suggest it would help not only my friends but the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite and everybody else as well. In my riding in North Vancouver there is a small jam factory at Gibson's Landing. Let me show what happened last year. Their total turnover for the year 1933 was $17,437. That was in a community of settlers who grow fruit to good advantage, but having no market they conceived the idea of a cooperative cannery for the production of jam. The farmers' wives and girls pick the berries and help to make them into jam. On that total turnover of $17,437 they paid this half baked tax of two cents a pound on sugar, or 82,320, and a sales tax of $1,046, representing a total tax of $3,366. Now that is out of all proportion; there is no

The Budget-Mr. Munn
rhyme or reason why a tax to that extent should be levied on such a small operation. The result was that after allowing the growers 4} cents per pound for their berries delivered at the cannery, the factory sustained a total loss for the year of $314.
Then take the proposed gold tax. I do not want to be personal, but that also is a half baked tax, and anyone who stopped to think would know that had it been carried into effect as proposed many thousands would have been added to the ranks of the unemployed. As regards mines in which there are high grade ores, they should pay an ample profits tax; but, I say, hands off the others, or you put them out of business. I am glad to know that the Minister of Finance has changed the original proposal which was absolutely unfair; it could not have been considered by people who are practical in that line.
Just a word now about the railway situation. I am one of those who have faith in the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian Pacific Railway has done a good deal for Canada but it has been well paid for it. I am not going to say who is to blame for the situation as it is at the present time, but in my opinion, to-day, we have in the Canadian National Railways a wonderful property, and all it requires is a square deal as compared with the Canadian Pacific. There is no reason in the world why this government or anybody else should get behind the Canadian Pacific Railway and guarantee its bonds, any more than they should for some private company that I might be interested in. As I say, the Canadian Pacific has done a good deal for Canada but it has been well paid for it. The shareholders of that company deserve no more sympathy for losing their money than I deserve if I lose money in my own business, or if any other hon. member interested in some business loses his money. I do not know why it is, but there seems to be in this house an air of friendship towards the Canadian Pacific Railway. It may be that a good many hon. members have stock in the Canadian Pacific, but they should forget that in the interests of Canada. The country has its money in the Canadian National Railways, and those railways should get a square deal as compared with the Canadian Pacific and vice versa.
I have on the order paper a resolution which I should like to read. I do not know whether it will be in order for me to mention it, but it is so far down on the order paper that it will not come up for discussion later in the session. In that resolution there is something which in my opinion is worthy
of consideration, and to conclude my remarks, with your consent, Mr. Speaker, I will read the resolution, which relates to the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. It reads:
Whereas, the attention of this house has been drawn by the royal commission to inquire into railways and transportation in Canada to the urgent necessity which exists for an early consideration of the capital structure of the Canadian railways (vide section 84-87 of that report), and
Whereas, that commission recognized that a very substantial part of the money invested in the railways comprised within the Canadian National system must be regarded as lost and that its capital liabilities should be heavily written down although the said royal commission did not deem the time opportune when making the said royal report to deal with this important matter but suggested that the same receive early consideration by the board of trustees, and
Whereas, a board of trustees has been appointed by the government:
Therefore be it resolved, that, in the opinion of this house, it is of vital importance that the attention of the board of trustees of the Canadian National Railways be directed to this matter and that this house deems it highly desirable that the said board of trustees shall consider this question and report thereon with the least possible delay as being of vital and primary importance in the intersts of all concerned.
