subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not going to discuss the resolution, but I want to say this: I am not one of those who believe that when you write off a liability you are getting rid of it; you still have it. If I were taking charge of a business and it were capitalized for more than it was worth, as manager of that business before taking charge I would want to have the capital assets written down.
I sympathize with this or any other government that is carrying on at a time like this. We are passing through very difficult times and have many serious problems ahead of us. The cost of government in Canada, municipal, provincial and federal, is entirely too high; we are spending too much money for government in all lines of activity. Further, we are paying interest at too high a rate.
The Budget-Mr. Munn

Other countries have converted their loans to a lower rate of interest and we in Canada should do the same thing. I do not believe in repudiation, but the situation is similar to that where a man in business makes up his mind that he can pay his creditors only so much on the dollar; it is better to take that than to lose all.
Then we have the unemployment situation, and many other problems, but one that worries me is that of the position of the young people who are growing up. I have not heard anything from government speakers which would indicate that any encouragement is to be given to these boys and girls in the way of work. There are many thousands of Canadian young people fourteen, sixteen, and eighteen years old and up and there is nothing for them to do. That is one problem in connection with which the government might do something. In British Columbia and other parts of Canada reforestation plans might be carried out; this is being done in the United States, and we might follow their example.
I had not intended speaking on the budget but I heard so much about the lumber situation that I thought I would give the house my angle of it. I have given positive figures aside from politics. If there are any lumbermen in Canada who have suffered, I am one of them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Under a Tory government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. The hon. member for Cariboo stated that since this government came into power the fruit growers and the dairy people in British Columbia have prospered. If there can be found a prosperous fruit grower or dairy farmer in British Columbia I should like to shake hands with him.
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Mr. Speaker, before I proceed with my remarks on the budget I wish with my first words to convey to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) my sincere sympathy in his recent sad bereavement.
A short time ago we had delivered to us a budget speech, and in my view;, after listening to the debate arising thereon, there seemed to be just two lines of thought in the minds and utterances of the different speakers. The government speakers carry us up into a new dawn of commercial progress, while those of the opposition, with the very same text, desire to drag us down into the valley of humiliation. The vitally important thought, however, as expressed in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, was the fact that

the country is now well advanced on the high road of economic recovery, and I am happy to say that this is borne out by facts, figures and present day conditions as they exist throughout Canada. The official opposition, on the negative side of the budget, seem to think nothing has improved, and take objection to the budget in all its different phases. It is, of course, the duty of the opposition to criticize; criticism when it is constructive and reasonable in parliamentary debate is part of our democratic form of government; but if we are to judge from the form of criticism displayed by the authorized critic of the Liberal opposition, the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), it is nothing more than a partisan, fault finding preamble such as has been delivered on more than one occasion in this chamber; in fact, it might be termed the sequel to the obstructionist tactics displayed in the house in order that the relief measure might not pass. The kind of criticism thus far directed against the budget is of no help to Canada's financial standing; neither can I see how it can be much of a political ballyhoo for the Liberal party.
It would be a long task to review the different speeches that have been made by opposition speakers on the budget, but the line of criticism was definitely set out by the authorized critic, the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth. They have outraged every phase of the budget, but what they are opposing is a budget speech that was remarkable not only for the manner of its presentation but for what it contained for this country. It is of such vast extent and vital importance to the dominion, and comprises so many topics that seem to create consternation among the opposition, that one even hesitates to enter the debate at this time.
Following the introduction of the budget speech the hon. member for Shelburne-Yar-mouth in a lengthy speech, made a very strong and bitter condemnation of the government. As I have said, it would be difficult to follow that speech throughout, but having listened to it and read it again I wish to make just one criticism of it: his speech might be well sized up as a political, partisan, dramatic extravaganza on an immensely stirring, thought-provoking subject like the budget. He presented his terrific broadside in the form of an ironic last act speech with the idea of making the house and Hansard readers believe this country was going to pieces-and you can believe it or not. The hon. gentleman's remarks and criticisms throughout did

The Budget-Mr. McLure
not add anything to the reputation for intelligence and vision of a political party over which it is his supreme desire to preside. Time will not permit me to follow in detail the remarks of the hon. member, but there are some points in his criticism to which I desire to call attention.
For instance there were some things that the hon. member shied clear of, whether consciously or unconsciously. At page 2427 of Hansard he twits the Minister of Finance with regard to his budget speech, especially his estimate last year of a surplus, which turned out to be a deficit. From that he branches off and criticizes the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) with regard to previous budgets. But I should like to point out to the hon. member that especially in times like these it is difficult to estimate exactly for a budget, as trade conditions are by no means normal. I might remind him that there have been other occasions on which estimates did not work out exactly. I would draw to his attention an estimate of his own government of the expenditure for the Montreal bridge- the hon. member was a minister of the crown at that time. They budgeted for an expenditure of eight or nine millions, but as a matter of fact the cost was nineteen millions and more. But there is this difference between the two deficits; the present government knows how the deficit last year occurred, but in the case of the Montreal bridge nobody knows where the extra ten or eleven million dollars went, unless the opposition themselves know. The public would certainly like to know.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Page Mr. Pitfield.
Mr. MeLURE: He may be in Newfoundland eating kippers. Again at page 2427 the hon. member for Shellburne-Yarmouth, dealing with debt and interest, gives a statement concerning the public debt, and then states that the increase in the interest payable by the people of this country amounts to $2 AO per head, and that the interest load which has been put upon the people since this government took office is practically $25,000,000 per year. He states that under the Liberal regime they had surpluses, and repeats the statement from the famous Dunning budget speech that Canada had a surplus of $257,000,000 between the years 1925 and 1930. I am reminded that in appealing to the electors during the campaign of 1930 that was one of their stock arguments. Let us see the story of this $257,000,000 reduction of debt which they claim. The Liberal government received during that time $45,000,000 from repayment
of loans and $102,000,000 interest on bank deposits and investments, making a total of $147,000,000 which came due and which certainly applied on debt-what else was there to do with it? Then there was a further $110,000,000 that they also claim they paid in reduction of debt. This came out of taxes. Why should it not have gone to reduction of debt? I might ask why they did not reduce it considerably more, in view of the large amounts of taxes they took from the people at that time. During the six years from 1925 to 1930 inclusive I find that the taxes collected by the Liberal government were in round figures as follows:
1925		 $293,000,000
1926		 328,000,000
1927	 347,000,0001928	 365.000,000
1929		 394,000.000
1930		 375,000,000
Making a total of over $2,100,000,000 in those six years. If we compute this on the systems the hon. member for Shelburne-Yanmouth used, instead of being $2.50 per head it amounts to $210 per head of taxes collected from the people to pay for the Liberal government's program of extravagance during those years.
Then the opposition critic veers away from the budget to preelection promises, and goes back to the campaign of 1930. When he refers to those campaign speeches and promises I should like to remind him that the government in which he was a minister came into power in 1921 pledged to reduce taxation. But what do we find? Instead of a reduction in taxation they increased taxes; they took from the people of this country more than $100,000,000 additional in taxes annually. Yet the opposition critic was a minister in that government; so I think he has no reason to talk about election promises.
The hon. gentleman attempted to show by a long parade of figures that debt and interest were increased by the Conservative party, and on page 2428 made what apparently he considered a conclusive argument. Referring to the Minister of Finance he said: "iMy hon. friend may say that this government's position is due to railway deficits." Then he proceeds:
Let me remind him that during the Liberal administration current deficits on railways were paid out of revenue, and were not added to the public debt.
This is new, and worth looking into. I am rather glad the hon. member mentioned these railway deficits, because as I indicated at the beginning I did not intend to correct all his
The Budget-Mr. McLure

misstatements but only to add a few facts which the hon. member had omitted from his remarks. From time to time the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth as well as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. He on an) and many other hon. members of the opposition have criticized this government and the Minister of Railways with regard to the railway problem, always blaming it on this party. It would have been just as well to leave out of this budget debate that supposedly telling argument. We know that the railway extravagance authorized by the Liberal government from 1922 to 1930 was tremendous. The railways were run purely as a political machine for the Liberal party, and railway construction and various other schemes cost the country over half a billion dollars, so that to-day we are saddled with heavy interest payments. These have been met and are being met by this government, and the credit of our country has been maintained at a high level.
Then from time to time the opposition criticize us with regard to the increase in taxation. The answer is that this is the result of the extravagance of the late government, and is necessary to pay their bills and the interest on the debts they created. We are taxed perhaps more than we should be to meet these requirements. But we might refer to some of their expenditures in connection with railways just to show that the opposition critic might have left this question out of the debate. Perhaps the most extravagant year of all was 1929; that might be termed their pork barrel year for election expenditures. Perhaps we shall be better able to appreciate the Canadian National railway problem if we look at the expenditures made by the Liberal government and consider a few of the things the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth omitted to mention, to show that the administration of which he was a member had no idea of how to finance. You might say that they had no more idea of the finances of this country or of the proper way to protect the public treasury than you would expect from a bunch of drunken sailors. I might quote the words of the Vancouver Sun of October 3, 1932, which, speaking of a Liberal ex-minister, had this to say:
He is an accessory before the fact in the economic ruination of this country.
Yes, my hon. friend the opposition critic neglected to say that the government of which he was a member placed an annual interest burden on the taxpayers of Canada amounting to many millions of dollars, and that the

greater part of the $57,000,000 that we must pay annually in interest on railway bonds is the result of the mismanagement of the present Liberal opposition. Let me contrast for a moment the political interference of the two governments in regard to railway matters. There has been absolutely no interference by the present government in the administration of the Canadian National Railways, but I do not think we could say the same thing with regard to the Liberal government. In support of that statement I would refer to paragraphs 61, 142, 143 and 154 of the Duff report. There you will read of the political interference under the Liberal government, when legitimate expenditures were ignored and the officials were forced to squander the money of the people in order to keep the political Liberal machine going in high gear. Let me read a part of section 154 of the Duff report, which says:
It is impossible to avoid the conclusion that the directors and management of the Canadian National were amenable to public influences and pressure which it would have been in the public interests to have withstood.
This portion of section 154 is well written; it is in good English, but translated into the vernacular of the day it simply means, "The Canadian National was run as a political machine for the Liberal party," and my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth was a minister of the crown in the government of that day.
Let us go a little further with regard to this railway extravagance. In 1929 they bought at tremendous cost fourteen million railway ties which, if laid end to end, would extend several times across Canada. I wish I had time to say more about these railway ties, but this was only one of the many reckless expenditures that were made. 'Sections 149 and 154 of the Duff report contain a severe indictment of the political expenditures made by hon. gentlemen opposite. In 1929 their committals cost the taxpayers of this country $270,000,000; in addition, the ordinary annual supplies for 1929 cost $132,000,000, and in that year they also purchased branch lines costing over $40,000,000. These branch lines were bankrupt; they never had paid and never would pay, and I doubt if their operating income would be sufficient to pay the interest charges. Then we had the Montreal terminals committal, to say nothing of the hotel and steamship undertakings.
I have heard Liberals, both on public platforms and in this house, endeavour to blame the railway management for this waste of public money, but the fact stands out like

The Budget-Mr. McLure
a sore thumb that the contract of the general manager expired on April 4, 1928, and was not renewed until September, 1929. The clear inference is that a club was held over his head and that if he wanted his contract renewed these extravagant expenditures had to be made in order to assist the progress of the Liberal political machine.
Now for a moment I should like to deal with salaries and wages. Hon. gentlemen opposite have said that under this government labourers have not been receiving fair wages. Let us see whether the labourer was protected under the Liberal regime, or whether they looked after the high salaried man. We had one man drawing a salary of S157,000 annually, with another man in the railway receiving $62,000. He was the director of expenditures; he had to see that the money went to the proper channels. Then another agent of the same bunch who was employed in London received $25,000 annually, and there were many other salaries ranging from $20,000 to $30,000. These are the people who, after paying these terrible salaries, say that at present the labourer is not receiving his just desserts.
The government made other wild expenditures. I would like to remind the financial critic that they paid $110,000 annually for club dues and fees. It would seem that the whole government were playing golf or that they belonged to all the clubs throughout the country. Under the present government all these extravagances have been cut out; no one can point to any expenditures of the kind that went on for several years under the Liberal government. Then there are one or two other salaries I should like to mention, one being that of a stenographer or private secretary who received $22,000. Do hon. members suppose that the Liberal party and the hon. member who acts as the financial critic for the opposition did not know anything about that? We will admit that $22,000 was a very good salary. Again, a policeman who strutted his stuff all over the country and was accommodated with a private car received a salary of $15,000. The cost of the private car in which he travelled, including attendants, amounted to an additional $35,000 annually. Under those conditions who would object to being a policeman in the employ of the Canadian National Railways when that system operated under the Liberal government? To indicate that the late government did not look after the interests of ordinary labouring men may I say that in those days ninety-six people were receiving salaries of over $10,000, and many
more were receiving salaries of over $5,000. This condition, I am happy to say, has been corrected by the present administration.
In those days they had all kinds of inspectors. For instance, in my own city of Charlottetown the railways had six or seven inspectors visit the city in one week. There was an inspector of spikes and bolts, another of oils and greases, another of safety-first devices, and several other inspectors attending to other minor details. All this work could have been done by one man. They had a good time, putting up at the best hotels and playing golf from morning till night at the expense of the Canadian National Railways. I believe that if the official financial critic of the opposition had looked into these details he would not have made the statements he did with regard to the Canadian National Railways; certainly he would not have said that they paid their deficits out of earnings. In fact it ill behooves the hon. gentleman, as an ex-minister of the crown, to jumble or to juggle figures with regard to these matters when, as a matter of fact, the government of which he formed a part were responsible for the greater part of the debt and interest of the Canadian National Railways.
Directing his remarks to the Minister of Finance, and speaking about trade conditions, the hon. member is quoted at page 2432 of Hansard as follows:
He does not seem to realize that perhaps the most important thing in this country is trade.
He stated further that trade had developed through its own natural channels. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member must have had a twinge of conscience when he made that remark, because it is not so very long ago that he was one of those hon. members who voted against the conference trade agreements with the British Empire. Dame Rumour has it that he has been severely censured by people in the maritimes for his action in this connection. Again, at page 2432 of Hansard he takes another wallop at the trade agreements when he uses the following language:
The fact of the matter is that any increase in trade between Canada and the Mother Country has been due to natural and economic causes.
I wonder if the hon. member will deny that the Ottawa trade agreements have developed a substantial expansion in Canada's empire trade. Liberal members will have to take back a good deal of what they said regarding the trade agreements. Their success

The Budget-Mr. McLure
has been a great disappointment to the Liberal opposition, and they will have to take a back flop in regard to many of their utterances in that regard. They wanted to destroy the Ottawa conference; they did not want it to be held. They have said that if elected they would destroy these trade agreements. I doubt it; I do not believe they will ever have the chance, but if they do, I suggest they would not dare destroy what has now built up in Great Britain a great market for our agricultural products.
It might be well to remind hon. members of the Liberal attitude towards the empire trade agreements. They dubbed the spirit of the Ottawa conference "economic imperialism" and "enlarged economic isolation," and declared that from the Liberal point of view economic imperialism and economic nationalism are both wrong. They further declared that Canada, as a great exporting country, must organize its trade relations on a world wide scale, and that anything less than this would be a denial of our birthright. I wonder how the Liberal party, its leaders and some if its partisan press will explain these astonishing utterances in face of the trade developments of the last year which have resulted from imperial conference agreements.
I could go on and quote from many speeches made by Liberal members outlining their objections to the empire treaties. The only conclusion at which we can arrive is, inevitably, that if the Liberal party had been in power the agreements would never have materialized. The advantages and benefits of the Ottawa trade agreements have been set forth and are known to all hon. members. In these days, when we are advancing along the highway to recovery, the empire agreements are of vital importance. Let me at this point mention some of the results.
I shall not go into details in regard to the dumber trade/, because that phase of the matter has been covered. I will state briefly, however, that lumber movement has been stimulated by the United Kingdom-Canada trade pact, and last year's trade was the heaviest which had been known for several decades. The export trade through the port of Halifax has increased by over fifty per cent since the treaties came into effect. A revival in trade is very much in evidence in connection with apples, farm products and steel products. Let me mention, further, the possibilities in -the bacon industry brought about by the advantages given in the treaties. The sure demand for Canadian bacon is 
bound to react more and more favourably on the domestic market. There never were more favourable prospects in the history of the bacon industry from the days of confederation down to the present time.
Again, the opposition critic severely criticizes the tariff policy of this government; but let us see what this government have done. They found when they came into office that during the Liberal regime Canada for a considerable period had been buying more than she had been selling; that Canada, in other words, had been a dumping ground for the surplus products of other countries, and the policy of the present government was to overcome that state of affairs. That they did by passing what is known as the dumping duty legislation. Instead of closing all our Canadian industries by its policies, as the Liberal government had done, this government protected our Canadian people and Canadian labour and Canadian industries.
The government has also been criticized by the opposition because it would not support the Russian soviet government plan. The Canadian government placed an embargo on the importation of Russian coal, Russian pulp-wood, Russian asbestos and Russian manufactured furs. Will any hon. member of the opposition dare say that these embargoes against Russian products were not in the best interests of the Canadian people?
I cannot understand how the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth and the opposition generally can continue to endeavour to mislead the public on the Ottawa conference treaty agreements, put perhaps it is only natural in their case because as they squint at the present and future, blinded by their own past record, they will always have a very poor idea of the present and of the future progress of this country.
Again, on page 2428 of Hansard, the opposition critic puts in what he again thinks is a stop argument when he says, "Someone else may say that the debt is due to relief." He had this question of relief very much on his mind. He goes back again to the election campaign, refers to unemployment in 1930, rehashes many of the campaign speeches about relief, talks about unemployment, quotes figures, and then proceeds to blame this government for the unemployment conditions which he charges have been brought about by government policy.
But let us look for a moment at the policy of the hon. gentleman and his government with respect to unemployment, and then contrast it with the policy of this government.

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
If you look over the conditions for the past ten years or more, or if you go back even further, you will find that from 1914 to 1920 prices and wages advanced very rapidly, with the prices of commodities perhaps holding the lead. There is no doubt that the peak of both prices and wages was reached in 1920. The decline of employment began in 1921, when the number of unemployed began steadily to increase. By the end of June 1921 there were, according to the statistics, over 100,000 unemployed in Canada, 2,000,000 in Great Britain and 6,000,000 in the United States. In the year 1921 there was available for the relief of unemployment in Canada $6,000,000, and the federal government aided the provinces and municipalities in all cases. That sum of money was spent by the federal government to feed, clothe and comfort the unemployed of Canada. Then in 1922 the Liberal government came into power and what was their policy with regard to unemployment?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in their opposition to
the Farmer-iLabour subamendment the opposition have made another faux pas, but of that more anon. It appears that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) was so convincing in debating the point of order raised by the subamendment that he may even persuade the Speaker to give the opposition's amendment a similar ride.
It was apparent, from the discernible apathy manifested by this house when the budget was brought down on April 18, that there would be no radical departure from the beaten path or from the course the government has followed for the past three years. Nobody expected anything else but a deflation budget, and a deflation budget it turned out to be. Outside of a few reductions here and there the traditional government policy of retrenchment and rigid economy has been strictly adhered to, while any desire to sail into uncharted seas, to seek new remedies, to live dangerously in order to live, has been frowned upon by the Conservative party which would preserve the present system simply by lopping off its mouldering branches.
The depression, sir, we still have with us, and the government's policies remain the same. The government still continues to try to borrow itself out of debt and to cure unemployment and falling prices and afford relief by the flotation of new loans. In other words,
it still continues to try to pull itself up by its bootstraps, which as everybody knows simply cannot be done. When one looks to the other side of the house for a solution all one gets is a lot of heat instead of light. As an example I shall refer to the rather unaccountable opposition of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to the Farmer-Labour subamendment.
Paradoxically enough the Liberals this session have out-conservatived the Conservatives and out-reactionaried the reactionaries. I shall leave the psychological analysis of this phenomenon to more scientific minds than my own. For the time being suffice it to say that the events of the past few months have more than borne out my contention. Pick up any magazine or newspaper in Canada to-day and you will read about it, or ask reporters and they will tell you about it, and it will not be long before Ripley will caricature this anomalous state of affairs in his "Believe it or Not" column. Indeed before very long I am afraid that both parties would be called the new Canadian Siamese twins, were it not for the legislation which the government has brought down in regard to marketing. If you do not believe that, sir, look at the columns of the Liberal wet nurse, the Ottawa Citizen. She ought to know, and after the way she has slapped the wrists of her nurslings I should have thought they would get wise to this, but as the poet says, where ignorance is bliss 'tia folly to be wise. If they still persist in running around in short pants and diapers instead of long pants, that is their business. If they have not yet learned that Queen Victoria is dead this debate will prove futile and will avail us absolutely nothing. And if Daddy King still persists in feeding his political children on the sour milk of liberty, how can you, sir, expect them to grow into healthy minded Canadians, with a healthy minded aspect of things and of life? I should prefer the raw meat which the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) feeds the brood on the other side of the house, even if it is not according to Hoyle. But the "Hush ye, hush ye, don't ye fret ye or the Black Bennett will get ye" attitude of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is the only type of food which the laissez-faire weaklings on this side of the house are getting from their well meaning but very unwise political foster father. It is no wonder this lack of proper food has produced such barren results in this and other debates.
Take their amendment. It was moved by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
on certain securities; and this in order to allow these companies to carry on loan shark business in this country.
All of these bills, as I have said, are similar in principle and therefore my remarks on one alone, that is Bill No. 15, the Small Loan Company bill, may be considered as applying to the other two. It seems that Bill No. 15 has had more lives than a cat. I thought it was dead, as it certainly should have been, and duly interred with a proper parliamentary monumental epitaph to mark the passing of what otherwise might have been an actual statute of Canada, and a very notorious one at that. It reminds me of the story of the man they could not hang, only in that case the man was innocent while this bill certainly deserves to be killed. It is like a weed; no matter how you try to dispose of it, the thing keeps popping up all over the place. The only saving grace about it is its stubbornness, a certain persistence that would do credit to a nobler cause. In view of the fact that this is supposed to be a year of great activity in parliament in regard to financial matters, and also that we have before the house certain legislation respecting the Bank Act and monetary reform, I cannot for the life of me understand how this bill was ever allowed by the committee on banking and commerce to pass the committee stage. If the committee allowed this rotten bill, as I might call it, to pass, then heaven help the bank revision and heaven help the central bank bill as well as any other pending legislation that was supposed to assist the Canadian people in getting out of the depression in which they now find themselves. Might I ask: Whom is this piratical bill supposed to benefit, and what good is it going to do in lessening the suffering of the Canadian people in this terrible time of stress?
I understand that someone in the committee twitted my colleague about not being able to legislate people into heaven and that he very pointedly retorted: "Not into heaven, but nothing will legislate them into hell [DOT]quicker than this bill." Upon an analysis of the various clauses in the bill I do not see how the average mortal is ever going to escape from the various tentacles that most certainly will envelop him once he is foolish enough to get caught in this bill, which I consider to be a trap to catch the unwary. It may be said that the prospective debtor knows what he is up against when he negotiates a loan under the provisions of the bill, but that certainly [DOT]does not excuse this house from allowing him

either wittingly or unwittingly to get into the clutches of the money sharks who are behind this proposed legislation. I therefore think parliament would make a very good start along the line of reformative and clean-up, constructive legislation by throwing the thing into the parliamentary debris and other rotten Tefuse instead of giving it a place of honour among decent pieces of legislation. The sponsors of these bills would have us believe that there is a bright side to the proposed legislation in that it would render a certain service. But this shining brightness in my opinion is superficial and illusory serving only to hide the dross underneath. I cannot help recalling an incident in my boyhood days that left an indelible impression on my mind. We were bathing on a sandy beach near Atlantic city when we saw a fish thrown out on the shore by a great wave. Try as it would to flop back into the water it could not, so it slowly died on the unaccustomed terrestrial domain. Some children playing nearby picked it up and threw it back into the ocean. Next evening we all went bathing again, when to our surprise there was this very same dead fish lying on the sand. It was one of those beautiful, rare, calm and warm evenings in June:
Then, if ever, come perfect days;
Then heaven tries earth if it be in tune,
And over it softly her warm ear lays;
Whether we look, or whether we listen,
We hear earth murmur, or see it glisten.
Well, we heard life murmur, but as far as this fish was concerned all it did was to glisten. A full moon shone on a cloudless and windless night. As its beams fell directly upon this dead creature of the sea they were reflected from its scales in multicoloured brilliance. The sight momentarily rooted us to the spot; then as we gradually drew nearer to the object from which it emanated and finally got near enough to pick it up, the offensive odour arising therefrom proved equal in intensity to its exterior brilliance. This happened about fourteen years ago. In my last years of high school I ran across a passage in which the orator berated a brilliant but corrupt man for something that he had done, in castigation of whom the remark was made that while the person in question was a man of brilliant parts he nevertheless was utterly corrupt; his whole action was likened to a dead mackerel cast ashore in the moonlight, shiny but smelly, brilliant but rotten. The name of the orator has escaped my memory but the picture has never been forgotten. Comparing that incident with the proposal made by the

The Budget-Mr. Buchkovich
bill to which I have referred, I might point out that while outwardly the bill may appear all right, a thorough examination of ite contents will show how really rotten it is. With all its brilliant exterior but offensive odour it has once more turned up in this house to worry hon. members and haunt their peace of mind. Frankly speaking, to me the whole thing is so offensive that it would only pollute our statute books to give it a place therein. Indeed, sir, were this legislation to pass I am afraid that turning to the page where this bill might be found in the 1934 statute book might be detrimental to the health of the prospective investigator.
An attempt has been made to throw a halo around this bill by referring to the illustrious names of the directors of the company. However, it seems to me that if they are as illustrious as they are described they would think twice before putting their money into a company of this kind. Why do they not invest it in government bonds, for instance? It would not matter whether the president were St. Peter, the secretary St. John and the general manager St. Paul, and all the rest of the evangelists, the board of directors, the obnoxious nature of the various provisions of this bill, the usurious practices that certainly would prevail if the company ever got a charter to do business in Canada, would still be reason enough to sound its deathknell. Oh for another saviour to chase the moneylenders out of the temple again! Let us hope in this regard that the Prime Minister turns out to be another messiah. It is beyond my intelligence sir, to understand why this fishy bill has been trotted out again to nauseate the house, when its only virtue in my estimation is a certain outward appearance that lends it a false respectability-the bright surface to hide a rotten interior; an honest face to camouflage a deceitful nature. I suppose the Dr. Jekyll brilliance has so overhelmed the sponsors of this and other bills and the protagonists thereof that they failed to notice the Hyde hideousness lurking among the provisions of the proposed legislation. But they might have taken some warning from the vigorous opposition of the hon. member for York^Sunbury (Mr. Hanson); for when a man so conservative turns his forceful eloquence against the dubious provisions of this bill I think it is high time for the house to wake up to the seriousness of what is involved therein.

In the face of such facts, Mr. Speaker, who will say that better days have not already dawned? In many respects the crisis of the past four years is comparable to the crisis of 1914-18. It has lasted for four years. We have been fighting with our backs to the wall. The resources of the whole country have been mobilized to meet the situation, and it has been met with the same high courage by all classes of our people, particularly by the rank and file on whom the chief burden always falls whether in time of peace or in time of war.
Another point worthy of comment, sir, is the fact that Canada's credit both at home

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
and abroad still ranks high; in fact there is none higher. This standing is not the result of mere chance; it is founded on two essentials, first the sterling character of our citizenry and second the nature of the leadership they have had. When the Bank of England ceased paying in gold, world financial institutions were rocked to their foundations, but drawing upon the traditions of the past and upon the strength which is intermingled in our blood, Canada stood firm. Again, when the United States issued an order closing all banks, in Canada the order of the day was "business as usual." Not a bank was closed. Canada's credit and the strength of her institutions stood out in those days like a beacon set upon a hill. Again this was not mere chance. All sorts of panaceas were offered, among them the suggestion that in view of exchange rates and certain general world conditions Canada should default upon her international obligations. That she did not do so is due in no small degree to the type of leadership she has had; I refer particularly to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Bennett) and his associates in the government. Theirs has been a leadership inspired by the character of our people. The stand was taken that default on international obligations was unthinkable, and to such vision, such action and such wisdom, Canada owes much. Already that is being recognized, but the wisdom of that action will become increasingly apparent in the years that are to come.
More important than bank balances is the matter of credit, either individually, nationally or internationally. What has this meant to Canada, sir; what will it mean? To-day Canada is regarded as the safest field for investment. We are a young country, sparse in population but rich in tradition and confident as to our future. The adjustment of domestic obligations, whether as to principal or interest or both, well may be made and in fact should be made, but in our international relations there has been no default and there should be no default. If honourable adjustments can be made in regard to international obligations then let us make them, but if not let Canada meet her obligations according to the letter of the contract.
The impelling reasons are practical as well as moral. To repudiate would destroy our international credit; to fulfil our obligations will set Canada's credit high. Any temporary benefit that might come from repudiation would be fleeting, but to fulfil our contracts will pay dividends throughout the years to come. This is not fantasy but fact.
74726-192J
Coming from Montreal the other evening en route to Ottawa I held conversation with a resident of the city of New York who has prominent business connections in that city. He volunteered this statement, "The United States has been watching Canada. We recognize, to an extent we have never recognized before, the standing of her credit, the strength and virility of her people and her institutions. When our banks tottered yours stood firm. When burdened with almost insuperable difficulties the words of your Prime Minister to the world were: 'Canada will keep her contracts.' The result is that prosperity will be forced upon you. I mean that the benefits which will flow to you from your stand will follow as naturally as day follows night. Our investments will come to Canada for her development because with all our experiments, the people of the United States are panicky. They look to Canada as the best and surest bet."
These days of depression experienced in the last four years are surely not without avail. There has been a reorientation of thought. Ideas heretofore considered too radical are now considered normal, when humanity is placed before money. It is now recognized that in our national set-up for the future provision must be made through planned insurance to take care of the sick, the helpless and the unemployed.
During these times what has been the contribution of the official opposition? Is it not opportune to ask what the contribution of the official opposition has been towards the solution of our difficulties? Any point of view put forward by myself as a supporter of the government is naturally subject to the discount of partyism. But let us examine the facts. Has the attitude of the official opposition been one of helpfulness? Has it been constructive or subversive? Let me refer to an indictment which recently appeared in the Ottawa Citizen, a newspaper which supports hon. members opposite. This article appeared in the editorial column in the issue of April 25, 1934, under the caption Negative Opposition, and is as follows:
There is nothing easier in Canadian politics than to sit on the opposition side in judgment of the government. The greatest opportunity for criticism is provided by the budget speech of the Minister of Finance. It is an opportunity also, however, for the leading financial critic to show where the opposition has any more hopeful policy to put forward. Never before in any Canadian parliament have there been such opportunities as in the years since 1930, but this official opposition has been more conservative than the government. It is simply
3038	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
a negative factor in parliament, offering neither light nor leadership in Canada's most critical period of economic readjustment.
It is, of course, possible to put forward excuses for the negation of Liberalism in this parliament. In the emergency session before Premier Bennett went to London in 1930, the Liberals could take the position that they would refrain from doing anything to retard the government's effort to deal with the unemployment situation. In the following session, they had the excuse of allowing Premier Bennett to demonstrate the futility of high tariff barriers in Canada. In the session of 1932, the opposition could continue to put forward nothing, by saying that the government would be allowed to go into the imperial economic conference with a free hand.
Last year, similarly, while the government looked to the world economic conference in London to provide the way out, the opposition had nothing better to offer. This session there is no such excuse, but Colonel J. L. Ralston's speech on the budget last Monday afternoon made it clear that the opposition sterility is due to something more than tactics; it is a state of political barrenness. The light of Liberalism is flickering so feebly on the opposition side, it is quite liable to go out altogether when the Liberals come back into office.
But, sir, we are rising above our difficulties. Surely it is time to move forward. Having held the line against all assaults, having withstood the impact of dire need and discouragement and having maintained an unbroken front, the time is opportune to move forward. Let me suggest to the government the importance of leading the way by immediate action by carrying out its tentative program of work, thereby giving employment to those who have held the line with such courage and high resolve, and replace this utter weariness and sickness of heart with hope and optimism.
I come now to Canada's future in the air. With what prophetic vision did Tennyson forecast the development which is upon us and to which I now refer:
For I dipt into the future, far as human eye
could see,
Saw the vision of the world, and all the wonder that would be;
Saw the heavens fill with commerce, argosies of magic sails,
Bilots of the purple twilight, dropping down with costly bales;
Heard the heavens fill with shouting, and there rain'd a ghastly dew
From the nations' airy navies grappling in the central blue.
It is all there, commerce and the emergency of war. Canada's future is inexorably bound up with the development of air routes.
At once, let me set up a background of fact, the reality of which can readily be demonstrated, against which to cast the shadows of things to come.

Flying is as yet a relatively new arm of our transportation system. Our people have not yet become air minded.
