speechtext:
It is but a little over thirty years since the first aeroplane flight was accomplished when Orville Wright made history by his flight in North Carolina in December, 1903. Little progress was made until after the commencement of the war in 1914, so that we might reasonably say that the aeroplane has been in use little more than twenty years.
While on the subject of early flights we should not forget to do honour to two Canadians who figure in these records, namely Mr. F. W. "Casey" Baldwin, now a member of the Nova Scotia legislative assembly, and Mr. J. A. D. McCurdy, now a resident of Montreal. Baldwin made a flight at Hammonds-fort, New York, on March 12, 1908. McCurdy made a flight over Baddeck Bay in the famous "Silver Dart" on February 23, 1909, Sir Elliott Y. Roe made the first flight in the British empire in England on January 8, 1908, it being an Englishman who made the first flight in the British Empire; a Canadian Baldwin, was the second in the British Empire and the first Canadian to fly. McCurdy was the first Canadian to fly in Canada.
It is a happy coincidence that on February 23 last, exactly twenty-five years after the

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
first aeroplane flight in Canada, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) presented publicly at Toronto the first comprehensive outline of a national aviation policy expressed by any minister of the crown in Canada.
It gives me pleasure to congratulate the minister upon his definition of government policy. In paying tribute to the Minister of National Defence as the one charged under the Aeronautics Act with the development of flying from the standpoint of federal government control, I am not unmindful that his predecessor, the present sitting member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) then Minister of National Defence, was also seized with the importance of air service to this dominion and worked hard for its establishment. I am happy therefore on this occasion to extend my congratulations to the member for Shelburne-Yarmouth and "to render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's."
On August 4, 1914, there were 272 aeroplanes available to the British army; at the time of the armistice, after thousands had been destroyed, worn out or become obsolete there were 22,171. In August, 1914, there had been less than 250 officers i.. this new service; in November, 1918, there were more than 30,000. In this almost incredible story of British achievement, Canadians played a tremendous part; by the end of the war one-third of the officers in the Royal Air Force were Canadians. Canada's share, individually and collectively, was out of all proportion to her population. May we not ask:
Does still the breed run true?
Does still upflame the ancient fire?
Echoing back there comes the answer of Canada's war pilots. A comparison of the number of aeroplanes destroyed by the four leading pilots of various nations forcibly demonstrates the high rank attained by Canadians. The four leading Canadian pilots destroyed 230 enemy planes; other British pilots, 192; French, 214; German, 246. Next to the number of enemy planes destroyed by the four leading German pilots came the Canadian pilots, and I think it is only fitting that I should put on record their names: Bishop, Collishaw, Barker and MacLaren; Bishop, with his 72; Fonck, the leading French pilot, with 75; MoCudden, the British pilot, with 54; Richthofen, with 80. And remember, sir, that these were boys whose faces still bore the soft and tender curves of youth which the stress of later years eradicates, but the memory of which mothers carry always in then-hearts.
It was not chance that wrote these results into history. The innate initiative of our Canadian youth, their environment backed by tradition, made such results possible.
Let us now consider Canada's position in commercial air routes. To realize Canada'f unique position in that regard, certain misconceptions as to distances must be at one. corrected-misconceptions arising from our usf of Mercator's projection in the matter of map making, which distorts areas in ratio according to their distances from the equator, Greenland, for instance, appearing almost as large as Africa. To get a correct conception of ail route distances you must measure them on a globe.
In considering this matter it is fundamental that we Should bear in mind that time has always been and always will be a prime factor in commercial development-in gaining trade and in holding it.
The shortest international air route from the chief centres of Europe to the Orient lies across Canada, passing over Newfoundland, north of the St. Lawrence, over Cochrane, Ontario, over Winnipeg, the Yukon, Alaska, and down the east coast of Asia to China and Japan. Now mails go from Europe to the orient by the eastern route, but when our airways are developed and we have a north Atlantic system the air mail of Europe going to the orient will travel over Canada.
It is in the northern hemisphere that the great trade routes running from east to west find the long overland stages. At the latitude of Montreal, about three-quarters of the distance around the world is overland. The desirability of land for landings, forced or otherwise is obvious.
So we realize-or do we realize-that if we take Chicago, for instance, as the industrial centre of North America, the startling fact is disclosed that the shortest routes from the centres of industrial Europe and Asia, to the centre of industrial North America, lie through, or over, Canadian territory? In other words, starting say at the Rhine valley, a great circle route would continue on through France, Belgium, England, Northern Ireland, the straits of Belle Me, the St. Lawrence river valley, through Montreal and on to Chicago-the important fact being that this route lies actually north of the St. Lawrence.
Again, let us not forget that history emphatically tells us that the flow of trade and commerce has always followed the shortest
3040	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
feasible routes. In this great circle route, Newfoundland occupies an important strategic position. Recognizing that fact, a determined effort was made by American interests through Pan American Airways to acquire vested and exclusive landing rights in Newfoundland for a period of fifty years, in consideration of substantial money payments. The agreement had been negotiated and was ready for signatures when the present government of Canada and the British Government, watchful of the situation, intervened, the results of which intervention were to safeguard for Canada and for the British Empire this important trade route that might otherwise have passed into foreign hands. This action was taken at the Airway Conference in Newfoundland in July of last year. The signifiaince of that conference will, I think, in due time be better understood.
Turn now to the orient. The shortest route from Chicago to Tokyo passes through Winnipeg, northern Alberta, down the Mackenzie river, through the Yukon and Alaska and on by the northeast coast of Asia to Japan. Planes from the Pacific seaports of the United States to either China or Japan will find that their shortest feasible route will be over Canadian territory, passing through British Columbia, through the Yukon, at White Horse, over Alaska and on to Tokyo and Pekin. Again recognizing these facts, American interests .have endeavoured to secure landing rights on Canadian soil along these routes, but again these routes have been preserved to Canada.
Whether, therefore, of our own volition or otherwise, we in Canada are going to find ourselves participating in important intercontinental air routes of the future. The significance of these facts will not be lost on this House of Commons. Canada must zealously maintain her sovereignty over all air routes which lie through or across Canada.
What would be Canada's position in the event of war? Aircraft must be regarded primarily as servants of commerce; yet our air transport system, while conceived for and serving commerce first, must take due cognizance of the possibilities of national emergencies. The only adequate defence against aircraft is aircraft. Without an adequate aircraft industry we would find ourselves in a hopeless position in the event of a national emergency.
To-night it is not my purpose to develop further the importance to Canada of the development of her air routes in the eventuality of war, other than to state that no good purpose can be served either in the
	, I
interests of national development or in the interests of world peace by emulating the ostrich and burying our heads in the sand, or by crying "peace, peace" when there is no peace.
It is important to look, sir, to what the other nations are doing. At this juncture we might well refresh our minds on the progress being made by other countries in the establishment and maintenance of regular air services:
In Great Britain, external as well as internal interests are being served by airways. Imperial Airways Limited operates two main empire trunk lines; one is from Croydon to Capetown, a distance of 7,945 miles, and the other is from Croydon to Singapore, 8,646 miles. This route will shortly be extended to Australia. The company is now operating a fleet of forty air liners and is doing a steadily increasing business, showing gains in every year but one, in total traffic ton miles. Figures for the past fiscal year show 2,100,000 ton miles as compared with 600,000 in 1928.
Under direction of M. Pierre Cot, the French Air Minister, the government of France has supported the amalgamation of five of the largest companies into one organization known as L'Air France, with a capital of 120,000,000 francs. In addition to a network of lines over Europe, a weekly service is maintained between Paris and Saigon, in French IndoChina. A service across the south Atlantic is projected.
The Deutsche Luft Hansa, which is Germany's national air line, also maintains a network of airways over Europe, resembling on a map a great cobweb, Germany itself being more extensively covered than any other country.
From Amsterdam, the K.L.M. Royal Dutch Air Lines operates the world's longest airway to Batavia in the Dutch East Indies, as well as other air lines in Europe.
Italy has six important air line companies at work, and their routes cover not only Italy but stretch out to Berlin in the north, to Barcelona in the west, to Constantinople in the east, and to Tripoli in the south.
Austria, Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Sweden, Switzerland, Denmark, are all relatively well to the front with air lines. Russia, of whom we have little authentic information, is known to have important trunk lines in operation, employing a fleet of large air liners.
Probably the greatest advance in commercial flying has taken place in the United States, and being a near neighbour we have more than passing interest in this progress. Internal interests are served mainly by three transcontinental lines. There are 19,500 miles of fully lighted airways in operation.
Externally, United States interests are being served extensively by Pan American Airways System, whose principal routes lie over the South Americas, the total distance covered

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
being 26,650 miles, and 139 air liners are in use by this one company alone. Their service, based at Miami, follows the east coast of South America down to Buenos Aires, then to Santiago on the west coast, and up along the coastline to a terminus at Brownsville, Texas. Having a large trade with the South Americas, the United States has found the fast mail, express and passenger services of Pan American Airways of great value.
In this regard Britain has found the air routes of the United States into South America of significance in the diminution of her trade.
Looking at the matter in the round, the big outstanding problem in civil aviation is unquestionably the institution of a regular air service across the North Atlantic by heavier-than-air aircraft. We must give credit to Germany for the remarkable demonstrations that they have given with the Graf Zeppelin to show that a service by means of lighter-than-air aircraft is possible. We must also acknowledge the work of both the French and Germans in spanning the south Atlantic by heavier-than-air aircraft.
The end in view, however, i3 to join the two important areas in the northern hemisphere-Europe and North America. A great deal of attention has already been concentrated on the problem, and five methods or routes have been proposed:
1.	The Arctic route via Greenland and Iceland, which is just over 5,000 miles from London to Ottawa. This route gives reasonably short stages and, therefore, would permit the carriage of a reasonable load, but it presents the very serious problem of fog and ice formation. It is an inhospitable route with very uncertain meteorological conditions, and durng the winter much of the route is a land of almost perpetual night.
2.	The direct route, flying from New York or Montreal to Newfoundland, and from there to Ireland, carrying on to London, whence air services radiate to all parts of the continent. This route is 3,500 miles, including a nonstop stage from Newfoundland to Ireland of about 1,900 miles.
At present there are no aircraft in the world that can fly this stage as a regular commercial venture carrying any pay load whatever, and the object of a North Atlantic service is, of course, not merely to fly it, but to carry load by it. This route also has to face the problem of fog around Newfoundland, and possibly ice formation in that region during winter.
3.	The Bermuda-Azores route, which is again about 5,000 miles, but which traverses an area of better weather and of less fog. The longest stage without the possibility of refuelling is from Bermuda to the Azores, a matter of over 2,000 miles. There again, there are no aircraft yet available that can fly this stage regularly and carry useful paying load.
4.	Floating islands are proposed as intermediate refuelling points.
If a satisfactory method can be found for anchoring these islands in the Atlantic, and if they are, in fact, able to stand against the Atlantic gales, there seems no difficulty in operating a North Atlantic service with their aid, if sufficient money is forthcoming to construct and man the number of islands required. The capital expenditure that would be required for the islands seems, however, to put this method out of court, at any rate at the present time.
5.	The last alternative is the employment of ships in place of the floating islands; to employ, in fact, the method adopted by the Germans for the South Atlantic service.
One would expect that it would be impossible to land a flying boat in the North Atlantic as a regular thing, even making the best possible use of the refuelling ship to form a lee. The method does not lend itself to passenger transport, however, even though the difficulty of landing in the sea close to the refuelling ship could be overcome. As you doubtless know, the method is for the flying boat to land on the sea, to taxi on to a trailing apron towed behind the steamer, and then to be lifted by a crane on to the deck of the steamer, and after being refuelled, to be catapulted for its next stage. The use of the catapult, involves, however, very rapid acceleration which would probably be entirely unsuitable for ordinary passenger transport.
It would appear, therefore, that we aTe faced with very considerable difficulties in the establishment of an all-air service across the North Atlantic. Nevertheless, with the progress of aeronautical science, the various obstacles to the establishment of such a service by one or another of the methods or routes outlined will in the course of time be removed. How soon progress will enable us to overcome these difficulties is a matter of opinion.
It is not enough that the distance shall be flown;-it must show a saving of time over the normal sea route, and it must do so at a cost that the traffic will bear, or at any rate will bear within a reasonable time. In the initial stages of any venture of this descrip-
3042	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy (Winnipeg)
tion, it may be necessary to foster the development by the grant of a subsidy.
Now, sir, what is Canada doing? What has Canada done? What should Canada do? At the present rate of progress on the trans-Canada system, there will be from coast to coast by next fall an airway on which safe landing places may be found at intervals averaging twenty-five miles. It only remains to equip this airway with lighting, radio and meteorological services, for it to be comparable in efficiency with any airway in the world. I quote from a speech of the Minister of National Defence, delivered in Toronto on February 23 last.
This work is being carried out by the Department of National Defence as an unemployment relief measure under the able and immediate direction of Major General Me-Naughton, chief of staff of the defence council.
Its importance is of the first rank. By this fall therefore the government will be in a position to call for tenders for better than a twenty-four hour transcontinental air mail service.
Time will not permit me to go into the present air mail services already established; they are considerable. The service from Montreal to Rimouski, put on during the period of navigation and inaugurated originally in 1928, is of threefold significance:
1.	Foreign mail via New York to Montreal without air service beats the St. Lawrence route one day.
2.	The Montreal-Rimouski air mail service wipes out this differential and ties the New York route. That means something to Canada.
3.	With the development of a ship-to-shore service, picking up the mail at Belle Isle and flying it to Montreal, we can beat the route via New York from one to one and a half days.
Then there is the Montreal-Albany service and the Winnipeg to Pembina service, connecting with all United States lines. There are also domestic contacts to all outlying points in Canada's hinterland and to the mining areas; down the Mackenzie river to Aklavik. There are two services from Prince Albert, one to Lac la Ronge and one to Isle a la Crosse. Coming eastward we have these services: Lac du Bonnet to Wadhope and Bissett, mining areas; Sioux Lookout to Red Lake and Narrow Lake, mining area; and the Amos-Siscoe route, which is also mining.
Then there is the bush flying of our trappers, miners and prospectors out into the hinterland of Canada. In this respect these pilots to-day are doing a national service to

Canada and are performing feats in flying which are second to those of the pilots of no other country. There is a winter service from Quebec to Natashquan and to Anticosti island, and a winter service from Leamington to Pelee island.
We did have an interurban air mail service in eastern Canada as well as a prairie service from Winnipeg to points in Alberta, which was discontinued owing to economic distress in 1932.
The cost of the prairie service came particularly under criticism. Certain extravagant statements were given wide publicity and should be dispelled. For example, statements were made to the effect that air mail had been costing the country $30 per letter. I find that the average cost of air mail was 47 cents per pound, a vastly different thing from $30 per letter. Even the somewhat experimental prairie run, which was cancelled, was doing better than fifty per cent of its cost. In that connection, too, one should bear in mind that the former service had no continuity. The prairie run was left-up in the air at both ends with contacts only through the United States. So, too, of the eastern section.
Of outstanding significance was the experimental ship-to-shore mail services operated under the direction of the Department of National Defence and the Post Office Department during the Ottawa imperial conference of 1932. Mail was delivered from London at Ottawa in less than four days, and vice versa. A three and a half day service between Montreal and London is an immediate possibility and should be put into effect with the least possible delay.
Is not this a most logical step to take particularly following consummation of the recent trade agreements with Great Britain? Let us more firmly knit the empire with another all red route. With the inauguration of a Canadian transcontinental mail service, the ship-cum-air service across the North Atlantic would give the fastest route from Europe not only to Canada but to many parts of the United States and to the far east-and, remember, through Canada.
In commerce, speed has ever been the mandate. The air mail is the answer to this demand for speed. Weighing fully the cost against the service performed, the air mail presents economic advantages of incalculable value to the nation. As one of the leading trading nations of the world, can we afford to ignore these facts?
Shall our transcontinental air mail service be undertaken by a private company under

The Budget-Mr. Willis
contract with the government, subject to essential governmental regulations and control to safeguard the public interest; or shall it be undertaken by a semi-national corporation on which the government shall have adequate representation, or shall it be undertaken as one more national enterprise? I merely point to the alternatives. But whatever the way, let it be one of planned progress, with adequate safeguards for the public weal.
We should now think of Canada as not 3,500 miles but as eighteen to twenty-four hours in width. Let us reach out and take our destined place among the nations. Opportunity is on tiptoe waiting to take off: let us give her wings.
I cannot conclude without acknowledging my debt for assistance rendered through the Department of National Defence by the minister and his able chief of staff, Major General Andrew G. McNaughton; through the Department of the Postmaster General by the minister and the officials of the air mail service branch. Particularly am I indebted for information to Mr. George M. Ross, executive secretary of the Canadian Flying Clubs' Association, who has done and is doing such splendid work in awakening and making our Canadian people air-conscious.
Out of all this welter of words, Mr. Speaker, this supreme fact overtops them all: Canada is on the Main street of the heavens. Would that I could splash it in letters of flame across the firmament! Would that it might stand out as a pillar of oloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, to lead Canada into her promised land!
Let Canada, led by her government, put her back into this development and make it possible to realize in truth and in fact the destiny envisaged in those lines:
Wider still and wider Shall thy bounds be set;
God who made thee mighty Make thee mightier yet.
Mr. ERRICK F. WILLIS (Souris): Mr. Speaker, for the few moments at my disposal I desire to bring to the attention of the house many matters which are of particular interest and concern to those whom I have the honour to represent. At the outset I wish to say that within the area from which I come, being the southwestern comer of Manitoba, there are very distressful conditions due to the fact that for the last four years there has been an almost entire lack of rain. No blame can be attached to lack of fertility of the soil in that area; no blame can be attached to the
people who live there, about ninety-seven per cent of whom are Anglo-Saxons from Ontario, but when for four years there is no rain, there can be no crop. At one time last year it seemed as though it were going to be possible to have crops in that area, but when the crops had grown to a height of some six inches there came from the republic directly to the south of us that tremendous pest, the grasshopper. Where perhaps on one day there stood a crop luxuriant in growth, the following day there were found only thousands of spikes, being the straw which the grasshoppers had left.
When people under such conditions face distress for four years, their reserves completely vanish and they find themselves requiring relief. Similarly the municipalities within that area have been able to borrow only that which the banks would permit them to borrow; they have then gone to the province, the province has come to the dominion and through these agencies help has been given. The physical hardships of the people in that area are of course tremendous, but I should say that they are nothing compared with their mental hardships. They are a people completely unaccustomed to accepting relief; they have lived many years without having to face such situations. They are entirely worthy; they desire to be self sufficient, self supporting and self respecting. They are, however, faced with conditions which are not of their own making.
It is strange that that territory in which during the years 1924 to 1928 perhaps the best crops in Manitoba were produced, has become rainless. I believe a survey should be made to determine whether that area is facing drought merely on account of a cycle which we believe prevails in some places, or whether there are within its confines many farms which are submarginal, by which I mean lands that will not under ordinary favourable conditions produce such crops as would allow the farmer to operate at a profit. Various suggestions have been put forward, for instance that a huge corporation might be set up which would take out of cultivation some lands within drought stricken areas, whether in Manitoba or Saskatchewan, with the result of course, first, that there would not be so much grain grown and, second, that a tremendous amount of hardship would be obviated in the way of people attempting to cultivate land on which it is not possible to grow paying crops. With regard to what is known as the drought area of Manitoba I think a survey would show
The Budget-Mr. Willis

that practically all those lands are capable of being farmed at a profit, because until the end of 1928 they were farmed at a good profit.
Due to conditions within that area the questions of interest and of debt are of major importance, and I am glad to note that further federal legislation is forecast under which there will be some system of debt adjustment. I should like to refer particularly to the good work being done by the present government in regard to the reduction of rates of interest on money which they borrow, with a consequent reduction in interest rates throughout the country. It is pleasing to see that treasury bills to the amount of
515.000.	000 were sold by the government during March, 1934, at rates of 2-85 and 3-12 per cent, and also that in April another issue amounting to 815,000,000 was sold at rates of 2'41 and 2-71 per cent. Last year, in August, for instance, the normal rate of interest was 3-75 per cent. Through what has been done in this connection there has been created in this country a short term money market, something which we did not know existed before. The old practice of governments was to call in the banks and the various loan organizations and to give them perhaps a percentage in order to sell treasury bills. Prior to 1933 the rate varied from four and a half to five per cent where the banks made the arrangements on behalf of the Canadian people. This year, however, the method was changed and the government sold treasury bills in units of 8100,000. They sent out questionnaires to all parties who they thought might be interested in buying those treasury bills. This has two effects: it will reduce the rate of interest and reduce taxation, and in addition it indicates the value which will come from the organization which we know as the central bank. It is interesting perhaps to indicate what the effect would be if we could place all our debt on the same basis. The funded debt of Canada on March 31 last was $2,858,000,000. The interest on that was $131,890,000, which indicates a rate of 4-62 per cent. If we could strike a new rate of 2-62 per cent there would be a saving of $57,000,000. There is due this year about $424,000,000 of debt. The rate thereon is 4-8 per cent, or a total interest bill of
520.484.000.	If we could strike a rate there of 2-8 per cent there would be a saving of $8,484,000. That is to say, if we could borrow at the same rate at which we have borrowed now, if we could carry that rate right across, there would be a saving to Canada of many millions of dollars.
In connection with the question of conversion loans there seems to be much mis-

apprehension with regard to the British conversion. We are often asked why Canada does not do what Great Britain did. It should be remembered that in the case of the British loan there was a clause in the contract providing that the loan should be redeemable at 100 after January 1, 1929. The issue was to run until 1947, at 5 per cent. The government refunded the loan as of December 1, 1932, at the same time offering to subscribers the right to continue their investment at 3i per cent, which proposal was accepted by 92 per cent of the holders. There is no such clause in regard to our loans, therefore we are not able to put through a conversion on the same basis as the British people.
I wish to turn for a moment to the general question of trade. It is important to note that we have no longer an adverse balance of trade. We now have a favourable balance of 8152,000,000 whereas when the previous administration went out of office there was an annual adverse balance of $127,000,000. This change is a tremendous achievement in itself. Another interesting comparison is Canada's situation in world trade in 1929 as compared with 1933. We find that during that time world trade as a whole was reduced by 68 per cent, the trade of the United States by 65 per cent and that of Canada only 62 per cent. These figures show that so far as world trade is concerned Canada has done better on the average than the world generally, and has done better than the United States, in spite of its N.R.A. and Roosevelt and all his great legislation.
Then I should like to draw attention to a question which was of particular interest to me and those whom I represent. Since this government came into power a duty of twenty-five cents a bushel was placed on corn imported into this country. I must admit that I had something to do with that duty being imposed; therefore I should like to indicate some of its effects. On March 1, 1931, when I made an address in this house in regard to the matter, we had on hand
100,000,000 bushels of barley. On March 1, 1934, according to the bureau of statistics we had on hand only 22,500,000 bushels, or less than twenty-five per cent of what we had in 1931. I do not think the question of price is a good indication, but I wish to give the prices. On March 1, 1931, the price of 3 C. W. barley in Toronto was 38 cents a bushel, on the same date in 1934 it was 54J- cents. But I think the most important feature in that regard is in connection with the importation of corn. Whereas for the twelve months ending March 1, 1931, we

The Budget-Mr. Willis
imported into this country 8,000,000 bushels to be fed to our cattle and poultry, during the year ending March 1, 1934, we imported only 3,000,000 bushels. That is to say, due to the imposition of that duty we have been importing into this country annually 5,000,000 bushels less, with the result that that market has been available to those who produce barley in this country, to the great benefit of the producer.
In connection with the duties placed by this government and the benefits of the Ottawa agreements, I should like to indicate the valuable increase we have had in exports of agricultural products in 1933 as compared with 1931. The products for which I have obtained figures are wheat, flour, oats, barley, cattle, beef, pork, bacon, ham, canned meat, poultry, eggs and butter. I have chosen these articles because they are items of importance to western 'Canada. In round figures the exports of these products to the United Kingdom in 1931 amounted to $81,000,000, whereas in 1933 they amounted to $99,000,000, an increase of $18,000,000 in those particular products alone. That is of some importance to the people I happen to represent.
It is often said by those who oppose us that this government is collecting too much in duties. In that connection I wish to give four different figures which I think of importance. -For the fiscal year 1923, when the previous government was in power, they collected in duties $133,803,370. In 1929 they collected $200,479,505, and in 1930, $199,011,628. This year this government collected only $65,900,000, in round figures.
Then it is often said that the policy pursued by this government of keeping the home market for Canadians had the effect of increasing prices. I do not wish to quote many items, but I obtained some figures from a store in my own town selling men's and boys' wear. I got the prices of twenty-two items as of June 1, 1930, and the present time, and on every item of ordinary apparel that a working man would buy there is a decrease in the price to the consumer. The items all tell the same story. We are also told that this government has strangled trade by the tariffs which have been imposed.
I desire merely to summarize statements which I might -make at great length, by saying this: In regard to our trade position so far as the world is concerned, aside from the figures I have already quoted, we occupy fifth position among exporting nations where formerly we were sixth. Of course the previous government .lost most of our export markets, particularly the United States where our annual agricultural exports totalled $159,000,000 when the previous government came into power, though in 1929 they had diminished to ten per cent of that amount.
I have indicated that there has been no strangulation of' trade due to the Ottawa agreements but rather there has been an increase, and that the increase in agricultural exports alone has amounted to some $18,000,000. I think it is well recognized by all those who care to read the statistics of the country that the previous administration, known as the Mackenzie King administration, increased tariffs. I have indicated also that in evidence of the fact that there has been no strangulation of trade we have a favourable trade balance amounting to $152,000,000 where previously we had an adverse balance of $127,000,000. In connection with trade it is well to recall that the previous administration was represented at Imperial conferences in 1921 and 1926 at which no agreements were reached and no progress made. It is also of passing interest to note that in connection with the Ottawa agreements, out of 228 items affected the tariff was lowered on 136.
From time to time we hear a good deal in regard to unemployment and the promises made in connection therewith. The promises made by the previous administration might very well become the subject of a forty minute address, so many were there of them, particularly if one cares to take the old platform of 1919. There one will find literally dozens of promises which were never carried out by the previous administration. In regard to unemployment, however, I should like particularly to refer to the fact that during the last fiscal year 250,000 more people found employment in comparison with the previous year. One could quote various summaries to indicate that trade has been increased and is increasing all the time. In one of the famous Southam papers of May 12 I happened to notice a list of improvements in trade, as follows:
The Budget-Mr. Willis

Toronto-The Ontario Paper Company this week announced a wage increase of 6J per cent for its nearly 1,000 workers.
Fort William-Great Lakes Paper Company, Ltd., is arranging to take on about 60 more workers and to operate three shifts.
Three Rivers, Que.-Employees of three mills of Consolidated Pulp and Paper Company in this district are receiving a ten per cent wage increase, effective from May 1.
Meaford, Ont.-The Meaford Manufacturing Company, Ltd., the town's largest furniture plant, is again operating on part time after a shut-down.
Hamilton-The Canadian Keystone Products, Ltd., is moving to this city and will manufacture cleasers and water softeners.
Marysville, N.B.-Canadian Cottons, Ltd., announce a five per cent wage increase for mill hands here. Plant is operating almost full time.
St. Catharines, Ont.-The McKinnon Company here, a subsidiary of General Motors, now has 1,290 on its payroll compared with 590 last year.
Ottawa-Lumber mill of J. R. Booth Company here, is again operating after a shutdown of 3 years' duration. The company will also operate a mill at Arnprior.
East Windsor, Ont.-This town's relief roll has dropped 2,300 to 5,776 in the last year, and reductions are being made daily as employment improves.
North Bay, Ont.-About 270 men will be given employment temporarily by the T. & N.O. railway, on track maintenance work.
Toronto-Canadian Frigidaire factory here has been placed on a 24-hour production schedule.
Montreal-Six thousand persons have been taken off relief lists since February and the number of families obtaining assistance is now decreasing about 200 -weekly.
These indicate, in any event, that there is a recovery going on, particularly in eastern Canada. But when we speak of unemployment it is well to remember that the question of immigration still has some bearing on the matter. I should like to quote two figures in regard to the people who were brought to this country by the previous administration. We find that in the year 1928 there were 151,597 people brought to this country; in 1929 there were 167,722 people brought here, but in 1933 we allowed only 19,872 people to enter Canada. That is quite important to remember when discussing unemployment.
Then for a moment I should like to refer to the question which Conservatives have to face every time they address an audience in this country, due to the influence of Liberal speakers and some sections of the press; I refer to the suggestion that the Conservative party stands for the big interests. I should like to point out that the financial centre of Canada is Montreal and that the financial province is Quebec. Montreal votes Liberal, and in the past the province of Quebec has

been solidly Liberal. Lately it has been slightly less Liberal; we now get a small block of Conservative votes from that province. The present government has increased the corporation tax, which affects all those in this country Who have money; it has increased the income tax on the higher incomes; it has increased the taxes on banks. It is bringing into existence the central bank, which is the greatest menace to the chartered banks that this country has ever seen. It has increased the taxes in regard to the carrying of newspapers, again affecting a big interest. It is said that the present government, through the measure providing for cooperation between the railways, has placed the Canadian Pacific in harness, or at least has had an influence upon it which no other government ever had. In addition this government refused to give the control of radio to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or other private interests. Of course there is protection, even as there was under the previous government; that is for the purpose of employing labour. It seems very strange indeed, if this government is linked with the big interests, that this party got nothing out of Beauharnois while the Liberal party received $700,000.

speechtext:
Not a cent. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, the clauses concerning the taking over of gold by the government and the issuing of currency, contained in the Bank of Canada Act, are the greatest blows ever struck against the banks, and the very investigation to which my hon, friend just referred, the Stevens inquiry, is the most courageous step ever taken in Canada with regard to whatever hold the big interests may have upon the country. Hon. gentlemen opposite were very critical of the government in regard to the gold tax, because the government preferred to tax those who had plenty in order that they might reduce the sugar tax which is paid by those who have very little.
The people are having great difficulty in deciding where the good old Liberal party now stands. Liberalism in this country is now a stranger mixture than ever it was in the past. If you consider the government of the province of Quebec you find the most reactionary government that ever existed in Canada; and that is the criticism usually voiced by those who try to tear down the Conservative party. In addition you have Liberalism as we know it on the Pacific

Sugar Tax Reduction
coast, led by Mr. Pattullo, who is trying to set up something in the nature of a dictatorship; he is referred to as the Mussolini of that province. Then, within the inner circle of the party we have the president of the Liberal Association for Canada, Mr. Vincent Massey, who since he made a fortune from Massey-Harris implements, has retired, and is now saying that the olive branch should be handed to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and that the Liberal party should be more socialistic. Then, solidly against that view we have the present right hon. leader of the opposition who thinks that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation should be wiped from the face of the globe. These are some slight difficulties with which the voters in this country are faced. The other difficulty, is, of course, that the Liberal government in the province of Saskatchewan will have nothing to do with what is known as the 'Progressive-Farmer movement, whereas in the neighbouring province of Manitoba it goes arm in arm with that movement. The old difficulties the Liberal party had were that they had in the west speakers who believed in free trade and in the east speakers who believed in protection. But in addition to the old difficulties there are the new ones I have enumerated, and we see others operating within the party. The result will be that when the electorate goes to the polls it will not be in a position to know whether the Liberal party stands for laissez-faire or old Liberalism, the reactionaryism of the province of Quebec, a dictatorship such as they accept in British Columbia; or whether they will follow those hon. members in this chamber who during their term of office secured high duties to protect the articles they manufactured. These are some points about which the voters will have to do some thinking. These are points which will be passed upon by them at the next election, and it is my guess that at that time the voters will decide that they had better stay with those they are sure about. They know where the Conservative party stands, and that is why I say that at the next general election they will turn again to the Conservative party.
